use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/application/MainWindow import MainWindowScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/harness-integration/baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/harness-integration/catalog import HarnessCatalogScope
from /scope/lsp import LSP
from /scope/open-projects import OpenProjectsScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/prompt-mode import PromptEditor
from /scope/prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/queue-list import QueueListScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /shape/ChatInput import ChatInputInstruction
from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export ui-component ChatInputScope:
    concept: {ChatInputConcept}

concept ChatInputConcept:
    pitch:
        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
        as snippets of Piton.

    shape: {ChatInputShape}

shape ChatInputShape:
    description:
        Input on the left, send button on the right.

        The body beneath the tabs has 8 pixels of padding, on the same flat
        surface as the selected tab, the ribbon's tab row colour, #333333 in
        dark mode, untinted by the mode, and joined to the selected tab with
        no line between them. In it, the text input sits in a dark box on the
        theme's darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, with corners rounded 4
        pixels and no border, as tall as the column
        of buttons beside it, 8 pixels from it, and taller when its text
        needs more. The text sits 8 pixels in from the box's top, left, and
        right, and grows down through the box. Clicking anywhere in the box
        beneath the text puts focus in the text, except while a preview
        shows. The preview shows in the same box, its content inset 8 pixels
        all round.

        At the right, a column of three buttons, 88 pixels wide, 8 pixels
        apart, each as tall as the input's single row: Send at the top, then
        Queue, then Preview, each the column's full width, flat, with no
        border or shadow and corners rounded 2 pixels. Send has a paper-plane
        send icon before its label, in semibold text, and keeps its split
        chevron, the send menu staying the only way to reach "Send to task".
        Queue and Preview are flat buttons on the theme's base surface,
        #444444 in dark mode, their labels in the theme's text colour, a step
        lighter on hover, doing what the
        send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that
        Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that
        Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the
        menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview
        shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also
        disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.

        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}

        Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. While the selected tab's lane is busy, as
        it says, the send button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs
        reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue: on Code while a task runs
        in the code lane, on Chain and Spec while one runs in the spec lane,
        and on Freeform while one runs in either, a Freeform task keeping
        both busy. Otherwise it reads "Send", so Spec reads "Send" while only
        a Code task runs. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is
        never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

    instructions:
        - @{ChatInputInstruction}

    sendOptions:
        splitButton:
            The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself,
            and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a
            menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right
            edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled
            whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its
            tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

        keyboard:
            <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input
            opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing
            while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the
            text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping
            around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes
            the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse
            anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking
            one picks it.

        options:
            The menu's options, in order:
            - "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
            - "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the @{PromptEditor} says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it
            - "Send to task", with a send icon, only while a task is running with a harness that can be fed more, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, and its output is shown, the previous tasks not expanded over it; never on the Ask tab, where a question runs on its own. It sends what is typed, and what is attached, to the running task instead of queueing it, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says, and clears the input as sending does. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) still queues, as the send button does

    editingQueued:
        Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the @{PromptEditor}, sets
        aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab,
        and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above
        it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text.
        Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads
        "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right,
        muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send
        button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and
        the send menu isn't offered.

        Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included.
        <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab
        selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it,
        cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as
        it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one
        isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in
        progress; so does switching projects.

    upArrow:
        <Up> in the text input, while it is empty, nothing is attached, no
        preview shows, and no menu is open to take it, goes back to the last
        prompt sent from the tab selected, as a shell goes back through its
        history. Anywhere else, as with text typed, <Up> moves the cursor as
        ever.

        On the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs, while the queue holds
        any prompt, it edits the last prompt in the queue, as editing it from
        the queue does, as Editing Queued says. While the edit is unchanged,
        <Up> with the cursor on the text's first line edits the prompt before
        it in the queue instead, and <Down> with the cursor on the last line
        the one after it, each cancelling the edit in progress first, as
        editing another queued prompt does; <Down> past the last prompt
        cancels the edit, leaving the input empty again. Neither goes past
        the first prompt. While the queue holds more than one prompt, editing
        from <Up> expands the queue's list, if it isn't already, scrolled to
        the prompt being edited, as the @{QueueListScope} says.

        While the queue is empty, and on the Ask tab, where nothing queues,
        <Up> instead puts the last prompt sent from that tab, the latest task
        in the prompt history, or the latest question asked, back in the
        input as a new prompt, as it was typed, with its attachments, and
        its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of its text. It
        is not an edit of what was sent, which has run: sending it sends it
        again as a new prompt. While it is unchanged, <Up> on its first line
        goes back to the one sent before it, and <Down> on its last line
        forward to the one after, <Down> past the latest leaving the input
        empty. Once it is changed, <Up> and <Down> move the cursor as ever.

    preview:
        Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the
        selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt
        included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the
        spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what
        the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's
        compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with,
        at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on
        macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a
        prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in
        place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up
        to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs,
        attachments, and send button stay as they are.

        The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or
        the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input
        would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape>
        goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they
        were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back
        to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

    tabs:
        The tabs along the top of the chat input, one for each mode.

        overview:
            The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat
            strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222
            in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it,
            between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in
            small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and
            its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, whether selected or not: Code red, Chain's
            icon purple, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. The one
            exception is Chain selected, when Code and Spec take Chain's purple
            too, as the chain says. The selected
            tab is marked only by
            its background, the same surface as the body beneath it, so it
            reads as a tab joined to that body; unselected tabs have none, and
            show the strip, lightening a little on hover. There is a tab for each of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and
            Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a
            small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against
            each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a
            normal tab.

            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together. Each open
            project keeps the tab it was left on, as the @{OpenProjectsScope}
            says, so a project starts on Chain the first time it is opened in
            a launch, and switching back to it selects the tab it was on.

            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
            Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
            not <Cmd>.

            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
            either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

        chain:
            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
            selects both Code and Spec. Its icon is drawn in Chain's colour, the
            purple of the @{PromptModesScope}, selected or not, as every
            tab's label is in its mode's colour. It never shows a focus outline, and its
            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
            is selected.

            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
            them.

            Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in
            combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all.
            Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a
            hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's
            pixels uncovers it.

            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
            Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background
            beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified
            tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code
            and Spec show through underneath it.

            While Chain is selected, the Code and Spec labels are drawn in
            Chain's purple, the same colour as its icon, rather than red and
            blue, so the unified tab reads as one mode in one colour. Their
            colour follows the slide: as Code and Spec slide together, their
            labels shift from red and blue to purple, and as they slide apart
            they shift back, each reaching its own colour as the tabs settle.

        help:
            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

            It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the
            @{PromptModesScope} says.

        session:
            At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text,
            sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a
            New conversation button. Each lane's tasks, and the questions of the
            Ask tab, have a conversation of their own, as the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, so the figure is the spec lane's on
            the Spec and Chain tabs, a Chain prompt starting in the spec lane,
            the code lane's on Code and Freeform, and the questions' on Ask.

            The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and
            extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal
            place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the
            harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new
            conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation
            was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many
            tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that
            the next prompt starts a new conversation.

            New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon,
            reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation
            for the selected tab: the spec lane's on Spec, the code lane's on
            Code and Freeform, both lanes' on Chain, whose steps run in both,
            and the questions' on Ask. The next run of that conversation, from
            any tab sharing it, starts a new one with no context instead of
            carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the
            conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but
            neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back,
            even once the project is closed and opened again, as the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

            It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a
            task on Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, or any question on Ask, without
            waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts
            sent meanwhile queue or run as ever, and the next task of the lane
            reset to start, whether sent straight away or from the queue,
            starts a new conversation with no context, the ones after it
            carrying that one on. That holds even when the
            running task is the first of its conversation and the harness
            hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't
            carried on either.

            Whether a task starts a new conversation is part of its prompt,
            recorded in its hidden anchor. Pressed for a lane with prompts
            queued, New conversation marks the first in that lane's queue, saving it
            again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation
            once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued,
            the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked
            prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or,
            with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. A task
            marked this way never carries on the conversation before it when it
            runs.

            <Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New
            conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the
            button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.

            Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut:
            "Start a new conversation for spec tasks (Ctrl+N)",
            "Start a new conversation for code tasks (Ctrl+N)",
            "Start a new conversation for spec and code tasks (Ctrl+N)", or
            "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in
            it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left.
            It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry
            on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next
            task, or question, already starts a new conversation.

            Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does
            beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives
            way to them when the bar is narrow.

        usage:
            Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the
            agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope}, has been used, as Claude Code's /usage
            shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the
            context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit
            nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's
            warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is
            reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is
            what this project's runs would cost at API prices, as below, such
            as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is
            written, when no cost can be worked out. Until anything has been
            reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.

            Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details,
            each group headed, and each figure labelled:

            \\
            - Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
              session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
              percentage, and when it resets.
            - Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
              and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
              what they would cost at API prices.
            - This project: every run the project has made, as below, split
              into tasks and questions, with its tokens by model and what
              they would cost at API prices.
            - The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
              last reported.
            \\

            A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather
            than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover
            says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs
            go, and from what it reported for the runs saved in the project,
            never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in
            place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking
            outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's
            tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it
            is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.

            A run's own usage is never the figures its result reports as they
            stand. Claude Code's result reports its `modelUsage` and
            `total_cost_usd` as running totals for the whole conversation, so a
            run that carries on a conversation includes every run before it in
            that conversation. A run's own figures are how much its
            conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run,
            each model's tokens apart; a run that carries on a copy of a
            conversation, as a question asked while another runs does, is
            measured from the run whose conversation it copied. When the totals
            went down instead, any of them, the conversation started over, and
            the run counts in full, as does the first run of a conversation.
            Runs are taken in the order they were sent, whether they were
            saved in the history or have just reported, so every run is counted
            once and no run's figures are counted again in a later one's.

            This project covers every run saved with the project, every task
            in its history, each step of a chain counted as a run of its own,
            and every question in its asks, not only those since it was
            opened, worked out from what the harness printed for each, as its
            record keeps it. It keeps updating as new runs report, each run
            counted once it reports, and a run under way not yet counted. It is
            split into Tasks and Questions, each giving how many runs there
            were and, beside it, muted, how many of them reported no usage,
            such as "42 runs · 3 without usage", the latter left out when none.
            Beneath them, for each model the runs used, by name, its input,
            output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, as the context figure
            writes them, across tasks and questions together.

            Cost is worked out from the tokens, at each model's published API
            prices per million tokens, which the application keeps for the
            models it knows: input, output, cache reads, and cache writes, at
            the 5-minute rate or the 1-hour rate, using the split between them
            the harness reports. Cache writes it reports no split for are
            priced at the 5-minute rate. A model is matched by its id, whatever
            date or context-size suffix it carries. The cost the harness
            reports itself, such as `total_cost_usd`, is never used. A model
            whose prices aren't known gets no cost, never a guess: its tokens
            are still shown, it is marked "Price unknown", and the totals that
            leave it out say so beside them. The project's cost is shown as a
            total, and beneath it how much of it was input, output, cache
            reads, and cache writes, each in dollars and as a share of the
            total, since caching is most of it. Beneath the cost, muted, it
            says this is what the tokens would cost at API prices, not what a
            subscription charges.

        slice:
            Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost
            button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as
            selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the
            prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its
            references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with
            the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it
            on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it
            is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt
            being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to
            the session controls.

        colour:
            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are not tinted:
            they stay the flat surface the description gives, whatever the
            mode, the mode showing in the tab labels' colours and the send
            button's. The send button's colour transitions smoothly whenever
            the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the
            new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing
            <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and
            <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey;
            neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from
            Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling
            its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code
            and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they
            have been given in the theme editor.

            The send button, both its halves, is a muted slate: the selected
            mode's colour, purple with Chain selected, mixed well down into the
            theme's base surface, so it reads as a quiet hint of the mode,
            about #3b4252 for Spec's blue in dark mode, standing apart from
            Queue and Preview without shouting.
            Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid
            hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or
            lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part
            them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the
            same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never
            staying solid across a faded button.

    systemPrompt:
        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system
        prompt is sent with it, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

    ask:
        Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the
        @{PromptModesScope} says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they
        all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one
        already running.

        Each question's progress and results are shown in a @{TaskTableScope},
        and while the Ask tab is selected, the body splits to show every
        question and its answer as a chat, in the @{AskConversationScope},
        beside the selected tab's contents, each new conversation marked where
        it begins. Each question slides in at the bottom of it as it is asked.
        While another tab is selected, the questions still running stay in
        view above the tabs, as the @{AskConversationScope} says, so none of a
        question's progress, nor a running task's, is ever hidden behind
        anything.

    answerSteps:
        For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished
        question's task table is shown, the table collapses the steps leading
        up to the answer, as the @{TaskTableScope} says. Tasks are never
        collapsed like this: see the @{MessageList}.

    askConversation: @{AskConversationScope}

    attachments:
        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.

        Images can be attached too: pasted from the clipboard while the chat
        input has focus, dropped onto the chat input from the file manager, or
        chosen with a small ghost button with an image icon, whose tooltip says
        "Attach images", on the tab row between the last tab and the help
        text, which opens the platform's file picker for any files, several at
        once, since the picker can't be limited to images. Pasting an image
        attaches it rather than putting anything in the text, even when the
        clipboard holds text as well; every image on the clipboard is
        attached, and a clipboard with no image pastes its text as usual.
        Several files dropped or chosen at once are attached in their order,
        each on its own merits. An image is known by its content, not
        its name, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP are taken: anything else
        pasted, dropped, or chosen, BMP, TIFF, and SVG included, is not
        attached, and a warning notification titled "Not attached" says it
        isn't an image. An image larger than 5 MB is not attached either, and
        the same notification says it is too large. A folder dropped or chosen
        isn't an image either, and a file that can't be read is not attached,
        the same notification saying it couldn't be read, and why. Each file
        left out has its own notification, and the others are still attached.

        Files can be dropped only on the chat input itself, its tabs, the
        attachments, and the text input; dropping them on the message list
        above it does nothing. While files are dragged over the chat input,
        its background is highlighted with the accent's fill, laid about a
        quarter of the way over it.

        An attached
        image's row shows a small thumbnail, its file name, or "Pasted image"
        for one pasted, and its size in pixels, muted, with the same remove
        button; hovering the thumbnail shows the image larger, at most 320
        pixels. Images and text are listed together in the order they were
        attached while the prompt is written. A prompt taken back into the
        input, as when a queued prompt is edited, lists its text first, then
        its images, each image named by its saved file, a pasted one
        included.

        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
        the attachments it was sent with.

    projects:
        The questions, running and finished, belong to their project, as the @{OpenProjectsScope} says:
        switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the
        questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The
        prompt being written, its attachments, and the Slice toggle stay as
        they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen. The
        selected tab is the project's: switching selects the tab the project
        switched to was left on.

    escape:
        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
        input. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) brings it back, from
        anywhere the chat input isn't beneath something else, as the
        @{MainWindowScope} says.

    growToFit:
        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at most.
        Its first row lines up with the send button, both at the top of the
        input row, and it grows downward from there.

    autoFocus:
        The chat input should be auto-focused.

    syntaxHighlighting:
        Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter
        Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

    lsp: @{LSP}

    harnessMentions:
        overview:
            Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@`
            offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself.
            The placeholder mentions both.

        trigger:
            A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after
            whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at
            sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference.
            Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after
            each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that
            follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger;
            outside of one they never reach the @{LSP}.

        offered:
            The skills, commands, and agents offered are the
            @{HarnessCatalogScope}'s. Each shows whether it is a skill, command,
            or agent, and its description as documentation when it has one.
            Results are narrowed and ordered like Piton completions: matches at
            the start of a name before matches anywhere in it, then by name.

        accepting:
            Accepting one inserts it as a mention, as the @{HarnessCatalogScope}
            says, in place of what was typed of it. Mentions work without the
            @{LSP}.

    hiddenAnchor:
        While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes,
        they'll be typing into a piton anchor with a userPrompt property,
        named after what the prompt asks for, as its naming says. It's this
        compiled anchor that will be send to the @{HarnessIntegrationScope}

        naming:
            Each task and question is named by the harness, rather than at
            random, so its files, its snapshot refs, and its header say what it
            was for. When a prompt is sent or queued, the harness is asked for
            a short title for it with the prompt-title prompt of the
            @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, in a run of its own that keeps no
            session, as the notes and commit messages are, with a small model
            where the harness can be told one. It is given the prompt as typed,
            and none of its attachments.

            The title becomes the anchor's name: its words, each begun with a
            capital letter, run together with nothing between them, keeping
            only letters and digits, as in ChatTitlesFromTheAgent, and cut at a
            whole word to no more than 40 characters. A name that would start
            with a digit is begun with Prompt. A name already used by a task or
            question of the project, in its history, its questions, or its
            queue, is given the lowest number from 2 up that makes it unused,
            as in ChatTitlesFromTheAgent2.

            Asking never holds a prompt up for long: it is asked while the
            spec builds ahead of a task, and a prompt is saved, queued, and
            compiled once it has its name. A title that hasn't come back within
            10 seconds, that the harness fails to give, or that leaves no
            letter once cut down, is given up on, and the prompt is named as
            before, Prompt_ followed by 16 random hexadecimal digits. A task
            cancelled while it is being named is saved under that random name.
            Until a task has its name, its header shows none.

            A name, once given, never changes, so everything that knows a task
            by it, the task sent to the other mode from it among them, keeps
            finding it. A task resent or sent to the other mode is named after
            the prompt it was sent from, its name without any number the
            numbering added, numbered as above, without asking the harness
            again, unless that name was a random one, when it is asked afresh.
            A Chain prompt is asked for its title once, and each of its steps
            is named from it, numbered as above. A message sent to a running
            task, which is not a task of its own, is named at random, so it is
            never held up. Prompts saved with random names by earlier versions
            keep them.

        escaping:
            A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it
            isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, colons,
            leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes
            all mean something. The anchor is exported, so that it compiles,
            and its userPrompt is a multi-line escape block, which Piton keeps
            exactly as it is: the prompt's lines, each at the block's
            indentation, fenced by a line of three backslashes, or of one more
            than any line of the prompt made only of backslashes, so nothing in
            it closes the block early. The systemPrompt is written the same way.

            Each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers
            whose first name is imported, in the userPrompt and then the
            systemPrompt, is also listed once, in the order they first appear,
            as an item of the anchor's references property, left out when there
            are none; a reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a
            pasted shell variable, is only text. `piton compile` resolves the
            references. What the harness receives is the prompt as it was
            saved, line for line, with each reference replaced by what it
            resolved to: a dollar-brace by its text, and an at-brace by a
            Markdown link, from the project directory, to the reference document
            the project's build writes for it, in the reference root of the
            config's first adapter, such as .claude/reference, named by its
            dotted path, and going to the heading for the anchor or property it
            names once the document is built. A prompt saved by an earlier
            version, as quoted pieces or as prose, still reads back.

        autoImports:
            The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there,
            typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the
            prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position
            for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other
            than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out,
            character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or
            brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment
            then never stops the server finding the names that need importing,
            both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

        attachedText:
            A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText
            property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the
            order they were attached, keyed text1, text2, and so on. Since
            attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each is written as a
            multi-line escape block, as the userPrompt is, so nothing in it is
            interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no
            attachedText property.

        attachedImages:
            Each attached image is saved in the project's data, as the
            @{ProjectDataScope} says, once the prompt is sent or queued, and a
            prompt with images gives the hidden anchor an attachedImages
            property: a list of the saved images' paths, from the project
            directory, in the order they were attached, keyed image1, image2,
            and so on, each written as an escape block as attached text is. The
            same image attached twice is saved once but listed, and given to
            the harness, twice. The images themselves are never put into the
            compiled prompt as text. The preview draws its thumbnails from the
            images in memory, saving nothing.

            The harness is given the images alongside the compiled prompt, in
            the way it takes images, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says,
            in the order they were attached. A message sent to a running task
            can carry images the same way, and so can a question. A saved image
            that can't be found when the run starts fails it saying so, before
            anything is run.

            Wherever an attached prompt is shown, in the latest task's header,
            among the previous tasks, in the questions of the Ask conversation, in the queue, and in the
            preview, its images are shown as thumbnails beneath the prompt as
            typed, between it and any slices, except in the latest task's
            header, where they come beneath the whole prompt, slices included.
            A message sent to a running task shows none in the task's output.
            The raw prompt lists their paths, as the @{PromptEditor} says. Clicking a
            thumbnail opens the image full size, in the platform's image viewer. Resending, sending to the other mode, and
            editing a queued prompt keep its images, and a Freeform prompt
            sends them as any other does.

            What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the
            attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a
            fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks
            in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the
            task's header.

        newConversation:
            The hidden anchor has a newConversation property, true or false,
            after the one recording whether it was sliced: for a queued task,
            whether it will start a new conversation rather than carry on its
            lane's; for the copy saved to the history, a task's or a
            question's, whether it did start one. A task starts a new
            conversation when it was marked to, as the session controls say,
            and also when there was none to carry on. Editing a queued prompt
            keeps what it says. A prompt saved by an earlier version, without
            it, still reads back, as carrying on the conversation.

        sliced:
            A prompt sent with Slice on is still written as the hidden anchor,
            which records that it was sliced, and is compiled the same way, so a
            prompt that fails to compile fails with Slice on too. But what the
            harness receives is the prompt as it was saved, line for line, with
            each at-brace reference replaced by the dotted path it names rather
            than a link, and each dollar-brace by its text, as ever. Then, for
            each at-brace reference in the userPrompt, once, in the order they
            first appear, what `piton slice` prints for it, run in the project
            directory on the source file and dotted path the reference names,
            under a line reading "Spec slices:". A slice that fails puts why in
            its place, and the prompt is still sent. Attached text follows the
            slices, as it follows the prompt. The system prompt is resolved as
            ever. A queued prompt keeps whether it was sliced, and the preview
            shows what the harness would receive with the toggle as it is.

            Wherever a sliced prompt is shown, in the latest task's header,
            among the previous tasks, in the questions of the Ask conversation, and in the preview, the
            prompt as typed comes first, with any text attached to it, and the
            slices are collapsed beneath it into a single row reading "Show 1
            spec slice" or "Show N spec slices", muted, beside a right chevron,
            as a table's collapsed rows are. Clicking it expands the slices in
            place, and it reads "Hide N spec slices" beside a down chevron;
            clicking it again collapses them. Each prompt's slices start
            collapsed, and stay as they were left for as long as the
            application runs. What the harness receives is unchanged.

use /lib

from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope

from /scope/harness-integration/catalog import HarnessCatalogScope
from /scope/lsp import LSP
from /scope/open-projects import OpenProjectsScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/prompt-mode import PromptEditor
from /scope/prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/queue-list import QueueListScope
